The three-vortex problem is modeled by a Hamiltonian system of 6 ODEs describing the motion of point vortices in a 2D ideal fluid.
The new reduction proceeds in two stages: a canonical change to Jacobi coordinates followed by a Nambu reduction.
The parameter κ₂ arising in the reduction determines the topology of the reduced phase space: spherical for κ₂ > 0 and hyperboloidal for κ₂ < 0.
Gröbli's classical reduction uses pairwise distances and suffers from singularities at collinear vortex configurations and lacks a standard phase plane.
The new coordinate system removes these singularities and provides a standard phase plane for analysis.
The conserved quantities in the system include the linear impulse M and angular impulse Θ.
The physical domain D_phys in trilinear coordinates is bounded by an ellipse or hyperbola depending on vortex circulations.
Collinear vortex configurations correspond to the boundary ∂D_phys and cause singularities in previous reductions.
The new reduction applies to the dynamics of three identical vortices and vortex-dipole scattering by a stationary vortex.
Invariant manifolds of equilibria in the reduced system correspond to boundaries between direct and exchange scattering solutions.
Changes in the scattering diagram as circulation varies correspond to bifurcations of equilibria in the reduced equations.
The Nambu bracket generalizes the Poisson bracket to handle multiple conserved quantities and is used in the second stage of reduction.
Jacobi coordinates separate center-of-vorticity motion from relative vortex motions, simplifying the system.
The total circulation Γ_tot = Γ₁ + Γ₂ + Γ₃ is assumed nonzero for the reduction to hold.
The reduced system evolves on a two-dimensional manifold, simplifying the original 6-dimensional phase space.
The great circle Y=0 in the new coordinates corresponds to collinear vortex configurations without singularities.
The Hamiltonian in the reduced system depends on logarithms of vortex separations and quadratic terms involving κ parameters.
The paper translates and builds upon Gröbli's 1877 doctoral thesis and Aref's trilinear coordinate interpretations.
The new reduction facilitates the use of geometric phase-space arguments previously hindered by singularities.
The scattering angle evolution equation is derived and integrated to explain vortex-dipole scattering behavior.
